title: Zooplankton Diversity Responses to Livestock Disturbance in Floodplain Lakes Under the Framework of the Dynamic Equilibrium Hypothesis
content:
ABSTRACT

Anthropogenic disturbances can strongly modify wetland biodiversity, but ecological responses may vary under different environmental and management contexts. Here, we evaluated zooplankton taxonomic and functional diversity in shallow lakes of the Paraná River floodplain from two systems with contrasting hydrological and management conditions: the Middle Paraná and the Delta region. We hypothesized that zooplankton biodiversity responses to livestock disturbance intensity would differ in direction and magnitude according to system-specific hydrological and management conditions, in accordance with the dynamic equilibrium hypothesis. We analysed diversity metrics and functional traits in relation to stocking density as a proxy for livestock disturbance intensity, system and their interaction using generalized linear models and piecewise structural equation models. S, abundance and FEve showed interactions between stocking density and system. In the Middle Paraná, increasing stocking density was associated with higher S and abundance, but lower FEve, suggesting dominance of functionally similar taxa. In contrast, the Delta showed declines in S and abundance and nonlinear FEve responses along the stocking density gradient, consistent with environmental filtering. Feeding type, reproduction type and life-cycle duration mediated the FEve responses, indicating trait-mediated effects of livestock disturbance intensity and system conditions. These results highlight that biodiversity responses to livestock disturbance are not universal but depend on the productivity conditions associated with the hydrological and management characteristics of floodplain systems, with trait-mediated mechanisms further shaping these responses.
